extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (real analysis / sequences & series) and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter covering tests and structural facts about infinite series (root test, alternating series test, rearrangements, Cauchy products, power series and radii of convergence, Cesàro summability, Tonelli/Fubini for sums). Aimed at helping determine convergence/divergence and properties of series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root test
rubrics_metrics.description: Let sum_{n=1}^∞ x_n be a series and define L = lim sup_{n→∞} |x_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 then the series converges absolutely. If L > 1 then the series diverges. If L = 1 the test is inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: compare with a geometric series. To show convergence when L < 1 pick r with L < r < 1 and use definition of limsup to bound |x_n|^{1/n} < r eventually so |x_n| < r^n and the tail is dominated by a geometric series. For divergence when L > 1 pick r with L > r > 1 and extract a subsequence with |x_{n_k}|^{1/n_k} > r so terms do not go to zero. The test generalizes the ratio-test intuition; use limsup (root) form for power series/radii computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating series test (Leibniz criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {x_n} is a monotone decreasing sequence of positive real numbers with lim_{n→∞} x_n = 0, then the alternating series sum_{n=1}^∞ (-1)^{n} x_n converges (possibly conditionally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses monotonicity to show even-indexed partial sums form a decreasing, bounded-below sequence and odd-indexed partial sums form an increasing, bounded-above sequence; both subsequences converge to the same limit. Provides explicit tail estimates: difference between partial sum and limit ≤ next omitted term. Monotonicity is necessary (see exercise). This test addresses conditional convergence rather than absolute convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangements: absolute vs conditional convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a series converges absolutely, any rearrangement (any bijection σ : N→N) of its terms converges absolutely to the same sum. If a series is only conditionally convergent, rearrangements can change the sum arbitrarily (or make the series diverge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof for absolute convergence: control tails and use bijection to ensure finitely many 'early' indices are included; use epsilon arguments to show partial sums of rearrangement approach same limit. Counterexample/illustration: the alternating harmonic series is conditionally convergent; by separating odd and even terms and rearranging (switching between adding odds and evens when partial sum crosses a prescribed target) one can construct rearrangements that converge to any given real number. This is an anti-pattern: do not assume termwise reordering is safe unless absolute convergence is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy product / Mertens' theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let sum_{n=0}^∞ a_n and sum_{n=0}^∞ b_n converge to A and B respectively. If at least one of the two series converges absolutely, then the Cauchy product series c_n = sum_{i=0}^n a_i b_{n-i} defines a series sum_{n=0}^∞ c_n that converges to AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: the Cauchy product is the sequence of convolution sums c_n = sum_{i=0}^n a_i b_{n-i}. Proof uses partial sums A_m and B_m, estimates separating finitely many terms from tails, and an epsilon argument; uses absolute convergence of one factor to bound cross-terms. Use B_max = sup partial sums of b_n when b_n converges. This is the safe way to multiply series term-by-term: require at least one absolute convergence hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: Cauchy product need not converge for conditionally convergent factors
rubrics_metrics.description: If both series are only conditionally convergent, the Cauchy product may fail to converge (or even have terms not tending to zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample provided: take a_n = b_n = (-1)^n / sqrt(n). Each series converges by alternating-series test but not absolutely. Their Cauchy product produces terms c_n whose terms do not tend to zero, hence sum c_n diverges. Anti-pattern: multiplying conditionally convergent series without further hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series convergence structure (radius of convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a power series sum_{n=0}^∞ a_n (x-x_0)^n, one of three possibilities holds: it converges only at x=x_0 (radius ρ=0), it converges for all x (radius ρ=∞), or there exists a finite ρ>0 such that the series converges absolutely for |x-x_0| < ρ and diverges for |x-x_0| > ρ. At the boundary |x-x_0| = ρ convergence must be checked case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the root test applied to coefficients times |x-x_0|^n to determine behavior. Examples: exponential series converges for all x (ρ=∞); geometric series has ρ=1; series n^n x^n has ρ=0. Endpoints require separate tests (e.g., alternating series at x=±1). Visualize with convergence-disk diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius of convergence via limsup root formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a power series with coefficients a_n, let R = lim sup_{n→∞} |a_n|^{1/n}. Then the radius of convergence ρ = 1/R, with the conventions R=0 ⇒ ρ=∞ and R=∞ ⇒ ρ=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: apply the root test to a_n (x-x_0)^n; L = R |x-x_0| and convergence when L<1. This formula is the standard method to compute radius of convergence; alternatively one can use the ratio test when that limit exists (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic operations on power series
rubrics_metrics.description: If two power series about x_0 have radius of convergence at least ρ>0, then they can be added and multiplied (by scalars) termwise for |x-x_0|<ρ; the product series is given by the Cauchy product c_n = sum_{i=0}^n a_i b_{n-i}, and its radius of convergence is at least ρ (may be larger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termwise addition and scalar multiplication follow from pointwise absolute convergence within the radius. For multiplication apply Mertens' theorem (since within common radius series converge absolutely) to justify the Cauchy product formula. Example: polynomials and rational functions expanded in geometric series illustrate these operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-test for p-series
rubrics_metrics.description: The p-series sum_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^p converges if and only if p > 1; it diverges for p ≤ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used repeatedly to test absolute convergence of series whose terms behave like 1/n^p. Example: the alternating series sum (-1)^n / n^p converges for p > 0 by the alternating test yet fails to converge absolutely when p ≤ 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cesàro summability
rubrics_metrics.description: A series with partial sums s_n is Cesàro summable to a if the averages (s_1 + s_2 + ... + s_n)/n converge to a as n→∞. Every ordinarily convergent series is Cesàro summable to the same limit, but some series divergent in the usual sense are Cesàro summable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises illustrate: the series sum (-1)^n is Cesàro summable to 1/2. Constructed examples show sequences with unbounded partial sums (e.g., spikes at perfect cubes) that are nonetheless Cesàro summable to 0. Use Cesàro summability as an alternative summation method when ordinary convergence fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tonelli and Fubini for sums (double series)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a doubly indexed sequence x_{k,ℓ}: (i) (Tonelli) if x_{k,ℓ} ≥ 0 for all k,ℓ, then the sum over all k,ℓ (under any ordering or as iterated sums) either diverges to +∞ or all iterated/reordered sums agree (finite). (ii) (Fubini) if the double series converges absolutely, then the iterated sums (sum_k sum_ℓ and sum_ℓ sum_k) converge and equal the same number as any rearrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: regard ii) and iii) as series of series and require inner series to converge and outer series to converge. Tonelli handles nonnegative terms (no sign issues). Fubini uses absolute convergence to permute/sum in any order. These results are discrete analogues of Tonelli/Fubini theorems for integrals.
